::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know how to use `filterFeatures` to filter DIA-NN precursor data by Q-value thresholds
- Know how to use `joinAssays` to combine per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` objects into a single combined set
- Know how to identify and remove contaminant proteins
- Be able to explore and visualise missing values in DIA proteomics data
- Understand how to filter sparse precursors based on a missing value threshold
:::

```{r}
#| label: load-dia-data
#| include: false

library("here")
library("QFeatures")
library("tidyr")
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
library("patchwork")
library("Biostrings")
library("stringr")

load(here("course_files/preprocessed/lesson02.rda"))
```

## Filtering (Part I): Sample specific quality control (FDR control)

Now that we have our precursor-level data stored in a `QFeatures` object, the
next step is to carry out data cleaning --- filtering to retain only
high-confidence identifications and removing precursors with excessive missing
values across samples.

DIA-NN assigns a Q-value to each precursor and protein group identification,
representing the local false discovery rate (FDR) at that score threshold ---
i.e., the expected proportion of identifications at that level that are
incorrect. Filtering by Q-value ensures we retain only high-confidence
identifications before proceeding to downstream analysis.

DIA-NN outputs several Q-value columns:

- **Q.Value** --- run-level precursor Q-value (FDR within a single run)
- **PG.Q.Value** --- run-level protein group Q-value
- **Lib.Q.Value** --- library-level precursor Q-value (based on the spectral library used in matching)
- **Lib.PG.Q.Value** --- library-level protein group Q-value

The output from DIA-NN contains information about q-values at different data
levels. As discussed in the main workflow, FDR should be controlled at the
highest data level to minimise the impact of FDR inflation during data
aggregation. Here, the highest data level corresponds to protein groups.
Therefore, we set a 1% FDR on `PG.Q.Value`, as well as the
global experiment-wide `Q.Value`.

Since our data was processed with match-between-runs (MBR) enabled, we
additionally filter on the library-level Q-values (`Lib.Q.Value` and
`Lib.PG.Q.Value`). When MBR is used, DIA-NN rescores identifications across runs
using an empirical library built in a first pass; the library-level Q-values
reflect the confidence of those cross-run matches and are therefore the most
stringent and appropriate filter for MBR data. We apply a standard 1% FDR
threshold (Q-value ≤ 0.01) to all four columns.

To remove features based on variables within our `rowData` we make use of the
**`filterFeatures`** function. This function takes a `QFeatures` object as its
input and filters it against a condition based on the `rowData` (indicated by
the `~` operator). If the condition evaluates to `TRUE` for a feature, that
feature will be kept; features returning `FALSE` are removed.

The `filterFeatures` function provides the option to apply a filter either (i)
to the whole `QFeatures` object and all of its `SummarizedExperiment`s, or (ii)
to specific `SummarizedExperiment`s within the `QFeatures` object, by passing
the name or index of the desired set to the `i` argument.

Since we want to apply the Q-value filter across all per-sample
`SummarizedExperiment`s simultaneously, we do not pass an `i` argument --- this
causes `filterFeatures` to apply the filter to every set in the `QFeatures`
object.

```{r}
# qc
qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ Q.Value < 0.01) |>        # Run-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ PG.Q.Value < 0.01)  |>    #  Run-level protein group Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.Q.Value <= 0.01)  |>  # Library-level precursor Q-value
  filterFeatures(~ Lib.PG.Q.Value < 0.01)    # Library level protein group (PG) Q-value


# check
qf
```

We can see how many precursors remain per sample after filtering by inspecting
the number of rows in each per-run set.

## Joining per-run sets into a single precursor set

After filtering, our `QFeatures` object contains one `SummarizedExperiment` per
sample run. To work with the data combined across all samples, we use the
`joinAssays` function. This merges all per-run sets into a single combined
set called `"precursors"`, aligning features (precursors) by their
`Precursor.Id`. Where a precursor was not detected in a particular sample, the
corresponding entry will be `NA`.


```{r}
# Total number of samples
N <- 30

# Number of replicates
R <- 1:3

# make combined precursor SE
qf <- joinAssays(x = qf, 
                 i = seq(N),
                 name = "precursors",
                 fcol = "Precursor.Id")

qf
```

Note that `joinAssays` only retains `rowData` columns that are shared across all
sets and have consistent values --- run-specific metrics such as `Q.Value`,
`PEP`, and `Run` are therefore dropped from the combined set. This is expected:
these per-run quality metrics were used for filtering in the previous step and
are no longer needed. 

We see a new SE dataset within the QF has been created called "precursors".
Let's check it contains the joined data.

```{r}
# check quant values
qf[["precursors"]] |>
  assay() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  head()
```

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=7}
plot(qf)
```

#### Removing redundant samples

When we have many fractions the QF object can get quite large over 10GB, quite
quickly. Therefore, now we have obtained a single precursor level dataset we
create a new QF object with only this dataset. This isn't strictly necessary for
this dataset, but it may be if you have a very large experiment. It also helps
to keep the object tidy and focused on the combined set for downstream analysis.

In the code chunk below we create a new QF object with only the final joined
precursor level data.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
## Identify which sets to remove
sets_to_rm <- which(names(qf) != "precursors")

## Now create a new object and remove them
qf <- removeAssay(qf, i = sets_to_rm)

## Verify
qf
```


#### Propagating the column metadata

The `colData` is currently attached to the entire `QFeatures` object. Later on 
we will need it to be directly linked to each individual set. So, we propagate 
the `colData` to our first set, so that it is carried upward and attached to
all future sets.

```{r}
colData(qf[["precursors"]]) <- colData(qf)
```

## Filtering (Part II) - Whole dataset quality control

### Removing contaminant proteins

In any proteomics experiment, some identified peptides will derive from
contaminant proteins rather than the sample of biological interest. Common
contaminants include proteins introduced during sample preparation --- for
example, human keratins from skin or hair, bovine serum albumin from cell
culture media, and trypsin used for proteolytic digestion. These proteins are
not informative for the biological question and should be removed before
downstream analysis.

It is standard practice to include a curated contaminants database alongside the
primary sequence database during the database search. For this data, we used a
modified version of the contaminants fasta from [Hao Group's Protein Contaminant Libraries for DDA and DIA Proteomics](https://github.com/HaoGroup-ProtContLib/Protein-Contaminant-Libraries-for-DDA-and-DIA-Proteomics/)
@Frankenfield2022, where we removed the contaminants from Fetal Bovine Serum,
which are not relevant here. The entries in this contaminant database are named
with a `Cont_` prefix, which is carried through into the `Protein.Ids` column of
the DIA-NN output, making them straightforward to identify computationally. In
addition to this external database, we also selected the "Contaminants" option
in the DIA-NN GUI. Therefore, DIA-NN also included its own built-in contaminant
database, for which all contaminant protein accessions are preceded with `cRAP-`,
again making these easy to find.

In this section we remove:

1. Precursor peptides corresponding to contaminant proteins
2. Precursor peptides which lack a master protein accession
3. Precursor peptides which are not unique to a single protein within a single
protein group

We can inspect the `rowData` to check the contaminants can be identified as
expected.

```{r}
# Extract the rowData
rd <- rowData(qf[['precursors']]) |>
  data.frame()

# Check for proteins with the prefix "Cont_"
table(grepl('Cont_', rd$Protein.Ids))
```

We see that we do have contaminants in the dataset. We will now proceed to 
filtering them out.

As with all data analyses, it is sensible to keep a copy of the data before
applying filters, in case we need to refer back to the unfiltered data later.
We therefore extract a copy of the dataset using `addAssay`, giving it a new name
that reflects the processing step we are about to apply. We will only apply
filters to this new copy, leaving the original set untouched.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Assay links
`QFeatures` maintains hierarchical links between quantitative levels, allowing
easy access to all data levels for individual features of interest. This is
fundamental to the `QFeatures` infrastructure and will be exemplified
throughout this course. When using `addAssay` to add a copy of an existing
set, the newly created `SummarizedExperiment` does not automatically have a
link to the set it was copied from. Where a link is required, it can be added
explicitly using `addAssayLink`.
:::

```{r}
# Add a copy of the existing data 
qf <- addAssay(qf, 
               qf[["precursors"]], 
               name = "precursors_filtered")
plot(qf)

# Add a link between the original raw and filtered
qf <- addAssayLink(qf, 
                   from = "precursors", 
                   to = "precursors_filtered")
plot(qf)
```

We now use `filterFeatures` to retain only precursors whose `Protein.Ids` field
contains no `Cont_` entry. We specifying the `i` argument to apply the filter
only to the `"precursors_filtered"` set. This retains the original `"precursors"`
set with all precursors for reference, while the new set contains only those
precursors that pass the missing value threshold.

```{r}
qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ !grepl("Cont_", Protein.Ids),
                     i = "precursors_filtered")

qf
```

We could also use the same nomenclature to remove precursors whose `Protein.Ids` 
field contains `cRAP`. For now, we leave these in so that we can demonstrate
manual removal below.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Why filter on `Protein.Ids` and not `Protein.Group`?

- `Protein.Ids` lists every protein in the FASTA that a precursor's peptide
  could have come from.
- `Protein.Group` is the group DIA-NN assigns after protein inference. A
  peptide shared between a contaminant and a real protein can be assigned to
  the real protein's group, so the contaminant accession never appears in
  `Protein.Group`.
- Filtering on `Protein.Ids` catches these shared peptides, which stops
  contaminant signal leaking into your quantification. It is the more
  conservative choice. The trade-off is losing a few peptides that genuinely
  belong to non-contaminant proteins, which is usually acceptable.
:::

#### Filtering out contaminants manually

If you didn't include a contaminant database in your search, or your contaminant
IDs do not have an easily recognisable pattern, you can still
remove contaminants afterwards. The example below shows how. We read in a
contaminant FASTA file, then identify and remove any proteins in the data whose
accessions match an entry in that file.

First let's load our contaminants FASTA file

```{r}
# load contaminant FASTA
cont_fasta <- "data/220813_Universal_Protein_Contaminants_HaoGroup.fasta"
conts <- fasta.index(cont_fasta, seqtype = "AA")

# extract contaminant accessions
cont_acc <- str_extract(conts$desc, "(?<=_).*?(?=\\|)")
```


In the next code chunk we define a function for contaminant filtering where we
identify any rows (precursor peptides) with a contaminant protein in the
`Protein.Ids` column and add a column to the data to indicate if a precursor
is flagged as a contaminant.

```{r}
# define function to find contaminants
find_contaminants <- function(se, contaminants) {
  acc_match <- str_detect(
    rowData(se)$Protein.Ids,
    regex(paste0(contaminants, collapse = "|"))
  )
  default_cont <- str_detect(
    rowData(se)$Protein.Ids,
    regex("Cont|cRAP", ignore_case = TRUE)
  )
  acc_match | default_cont
}
```

Now we run this function on our dataset to identify any contaminant matches

```{r}
# create a new object called `cont_tf`
cont_tf <- 
  find_contaminants(se = qf[["precursors_filtered"]], 
                    contaminants = cont_acc)

table(cont_tf)
```



::: {.callout-exercise}
#### Challenge: Manual filtering of remaining contaminants

{{< level 2 >}}

1. Create a column called `is_contaminant` that can be used with the `filterFeatures`
function.

2. Use the newly created `is_contaminant` column in the `rowData` to remove any
precursors which match a protein accession in the manually imported contaminant
fasta.


::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"}

**Task 1**
The `filterFeatures` function carries out conditional filtering based on columns
within the `rowData`. So, we add a new column to the `rowData` called `is_contaminant` 
which we can now filter on.

```{r}
rowData(qf[["precursors_filtered"]])$is_contaminant <- cont_tf
```

Let's check our `is_contaminant` column has been successfully created.

```{r}
# Check it has been created
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |> 
  rowData() |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  pull(is_contaminant) |> 
  table()
```

Let's look at some of these proteins.

```{r}
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |> 
  rowData() |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  filter(is_contaminant == TRUE) |>
  dplyr::select(Protein.Ids, Protein.Group)
```

As expected, these are the contaminant proteins from DIA-NNs built-in database
that contain `cRAP`. 

**Task 2**
Now we can easily apply `filterFeatures` as we have before. 

```{r}
#| label: filter out contaminants
qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ !is_contaminant, 
                 i = "precursors_filtered")

qf
```

:::::
:::

### Removal of peptides with no protein assignment

Since the analysis will be carried out at the protein-level, we will need to
aggregate precursor peptides into their corresponding proteins. Precursor
entries which lack protein assignment cannot be used and must be removed.

Let's see if we have any such precursors in the dataset.

```{r}
qf[["precursors_filtered"]] |>
  rowData() |> 
  as_tibble() |> 
  pull(Protein.Ids) |>
  anyNA()
```

This data does not contain any precursor peptides without a protein assignment,
so we don't have to remove any here.

### Removal of shared peptides

As well as removing precursors without a protein assignment, we also wish to
remove precursor peptides which are assigned to multiple proteins. Although most
precursor peptides have a single accession in the `Protein.Ids` column, there
are some precursors for which this column contains multiple accessions separated
by a `;`. Since the output does not contain a column to specifically tell us how
many proteins a peptide is mapped to, we take advantage of the `;` and remove
all rows (precursors) with a `;` in the `Protein.Ids` column.

```{r}
qf <- qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ !str_detect(Protein.Ids, ";"),
                 i = "precursors_filtered")

qf
```


```{r}
#| label: create-final-filtered-dataset
#| include: false

save(qf, file = here("course_files/preprocessed/lesson03.rda"))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- DIA-NN Q-value columns (`Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`, `Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) represent the local FDR for each identification; filtering at ≤ 0.01 retains only identifications at 1% FDR
- When match-between-runs is enabled, library-level Q-values (`Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) are the most appropriate filter as they reflect the confidence of cross-run matches
- `filterFeatures` applies row-level filters based on `rowData` variables, and can be applied to the whole `QFeatures` object or to specific sets
- Contaminant proteins (e.g., keratins, trypsin, BSA) should be removed before downstream analysis; including a curated contaminant database in the search and filtering on a `Cont_` prefix in `Protein.Ids` is a straightforward way to do this
- `joinAssays` combines per-sample `SummarizedExperiment` objects into a single combined set, with missing values (`NA`) where a precursor was not detected in a given sample
:::
